# Chapter 1 — What Philosophy Is, and What It Is For

> “The value of philosophy is, in fact, to be sought largely in its very uncertainty. The man who has no tincture of philosophy goes through life imprisoned in the prejudices derived from common sense, from the habitual beliefs of his age or his nation, and from convictions which have grown up in his mind without the co-operation or consent of his deliberate reason.”
> — Bertrand Russell, *The Problems of Philosophy*, Ch. XV

---

## 1. The Naive Picture, and Why It Fails

Begin with a scene that will be familiar to anyone who has taught the subject. A student arrives at the first lecture expecting to be told the answers. When she is instead given two incompatible answers, each defended with care, she concludes — politely but firmly — that philosophy is a matter of opinion. “That’s just, like, your perspective.” She has not been persuaded by an argument; she has been disappointed by the absence of a verdict.

This is the **naive picture**: philosophy is a catalogue of worldviews. There are Platonists, Aristotelians, Cartesians, Kantians, Utilitarians, Existentialists; each has a system; you choose one the way you choose a political party or a football team. On this picture, the history of philosophy is a museum of incompatible doctrines, and the activity of philosophy is the activity of picking a room in the museum and settling in.

The naive picture is not stupid. It is the natural inference from three genuine features of the discipline:

1. **Philosophy contains real, unresolved disagreement**, and this disagreement is not merely a matter of ignorance awaiting data. Two philosophers of equal brilliance and equal information can disagree about free will forever.
2. **Philosophy has no agreed method of adjudication.** There is no experiment that settles whether the will is free, no measurement that decides whether numbers exist.
3. **Philosophy’s answers are entangled with the philosopher’s values, history, and temperament** in ways that scientific answers are supposed not to be.

Each of these is true. Together they seem to force the conclusion that philosophy is opinion. But the inference is invalid, and seeing why is the first lesson of the subject.

**First error: confusing the question with the answer.** “What is justice?” is not the same kind of thing as “Justice is the interest of the stronger” (Thrasymachus) or “Justice is the health of the soul” (Plato). The question has a structure; the answers are candidates; and candidates can be evaluated — for consistency, for explanatory power, for fidelity to the phenomena they purport to explain — *without our having a decisive verdict*. That a jury cannot reach a verdict does not make the trial a matter of taste. It makes it a hard trial.

**Second error: treating disagreement as evidence of arbitrariness.** Disagreement is evidence of *difficulty*, not of *subjectivity*, unless we have independent reason to think that agreement would have been forthcoming if there were a fact of the matter. In the sciences, disagreement is normally local and temporary; in philosophy it is global and durable. That difference is real and must be explained. But the explanation might be that philosophical questions are *harder*, or *more general*, or *more closely tied to the whole of our framework of belief* — not that they have no answers. Compare: there is durable, global disagreement about how to raise children, and yet some ways of raising children are clearly worse than others. Durability of disagreement underdetermines the metaphysics.

**Third error: mistaking the sociology for the content.** That philosophy is *practised* by people with temperaments, in departments with politics, in cultures with histories, is a fact about philosophers. It does not follow that the *propositions they assert* are merely expressions of those facts. This is a special case of a general fallacy: the genetic fallacy, the confusion of an account of a belief’s *origin* with an account of its *warrant*. (We will return to this in §5 and again in Ch. 3, §5, when we discuss genealogical debunking.)

There is, however, a fourth feature of philosophy that the naive picture gets right and that any honest account must accommodate: **philosophy is reflexive in a way the sciences are not.** The physicist can take for granted what physics is, what a theory is, what evidence is, and what it is for one theory to be better than another. The philosopher cannot take these for granted, because they are among her questions. This reflexivity is the source of philosophy’s peculiar difficulty — and of its peculiar value. It is also the reason philosophy so often *looks* like opinion from the outside: it is the discipline in which the standards of assessment are themselves on the table.

So the naive picture fails. But it fails for a reason that points toward the right picture. If philosophy is not a catalogue of opinions, what is it?

---

## 2. Three Working Definitions

Philosophers have proposed many definitions of their subject. Three are worth distinguishing, because they correspond to three genuine and complementary conceptions of the activity, and because this book uses all three.

### (a) Philosophy as conceptual analysis

The classical conception: philosophy’s job is to analyse concepts — to give necessary and sufficient conditions for their application. What is *knowledge*? What is *causation*? What is *justice*? What is a *person*? On this view, the philosopher’s characteristic product is a biconditional:

> $x$ is a $K$ if and only if $x$ is $F_1$ and $F_2$ and … and $F_n$.

The model has real virtues. It explains why philosophy can deliver *a priori* knowledge (Ch. 9): if you are analysing a concept you already possess, you do not need to go and look at the world. It explains why conceptual analysis feels like *discovery* rather than *invention*. And it has produced some of philosophy’s most durable achievements — the analysis of knowledge in the *Theaetetus*, the theory of descriptions (Ch. 12), the distinction between *de dicto* and *de re* modality (Ch. 16).

It also has well-known vices, which the book will treat in detail (Ch. 3, §1):

- **The classical model is probably false for most interesting concepts.** Since Gettier (1963), we know that “justified true belief” is not sufficient for knowledge (Ch. 7). Since Wittgenstein and Quine, we have reason to doubt that most concepts have sharp necessary-and-sufficient conditions at all. Many are prototypes, clusters, family-resemblance structures, or essentially contested.
- **Analysis tends to be either trivial or revisionary.** If the analysans is synonymous with the analysandum, the analysis is uninformative; if it is not, it is not analysis but *replacement* — conceptual engineering rather than conceptual analysis (Ch. 33, §4).
- **The method of cases is empirically fragile.** Experimental philosophy has shown that intuitions about cases vary with culture, order of presentation, and affect (Ch. 3, §6; Ch. 9, §4).

Still, the impulse behind conceptual analysis is sound and ineliminable: before we can say whether there is knowledge, or whether justice requires equality, we need to know what we are talking about. The book therefore keeps conceptual analysis as one instrument among others, not as the whole toolkit.

### (b) Philosophy as rational reconstruction

A second conception: philosophy makes explicit the principles that are *implicit* in a practice. We already reason scientifically, morally, mathematically, and linguistically; the philosopher’s task is to reconstruct the rules we are following, the commitments we are incurring, and the structure that our practice presupposes.

This is the conception behind Carnap’s *logical syntax*, behind the formal semantics of natural language (Ch. 31), behind decision theory and Bayesian epistemology (Ch. 10), behind Rawls’s construction of a “basic structure” and a veil of ignorance (Ch. 47), and behind the contemporary project of *conceptual engineering* (Ch. 33, §4). Its characteristic question is not “What does *knowledge* mean?” but “What would a system of belief-forming processes have to be like for it to be truth-conducive, and how do our actual processes compare?”

Rational reconstruction is powerful because it is *accountable*: a reconstruction can be tested against the practice it reconstructs. If your theory of assertion implies that most of what we say is not assertion, so much the worse for your theory. It is also the conception that most naturally connects philosophy to the special sciences, since the practices being reconstructed are often the practices of physicists, biologists, or statisticians (Part VI).

Its danger is that reconstruction can become *legislation*: the philosopher tells the practice what it must be, and when the practice refuses, the philosopher concludes that the practice is confused. Sometimes this is right — the practice *is* confused. But the burden of proof is on the reconstructor, and it is heavy.

### (c) Philosophy as the study of the conditions of intelligibility

The third conception, and the one this book adopts as its working definition, is broader than either of the first two. Philosophy is the study of **what would have to be the case — what we would have to show, say, and assume — for our ordinary beliefs, concepts, and practices to be coherent.**

This is a descendant of Kant’s transcendental question (“What are the conditions of the possibility of experience?”), but it is *naturalized*: it does not appeal to a mysterious faculty of pure reason, and it does not assume that the conditions it finds will be a priori or necessary. It asks, of any domain of human thought:

- What are the **presuppositions** of this practice? (For there to be promises, there must be conventions; for there to be assertions, there must be norms of truthfulness; for there to be property, there must be a system of recognition.)
- What are the **commitments** of this belief? (If determinism is true, what follows for responsibility? If physicalism is true, what follows for the causal efficacy of the mental?)
- What are the **limits** of this concept? (Where does “cause” stop applying? Where does “person” run out? What is the difference between a deep question and a pseudo-question?)
- What would **coherence** require? (Can I hold this belief together with that one? If not, which gives way?)

The advantage of this formulation is that it covers the whole of the book without dissolving its unity. Conceptual analysis is the special case where the practice being studied is *concept application*. Rational reconstruction is the special case where the practice is *inference*. The conditions-of-intelligibility formulation also makes room for the parts of philosophy that are not analysis at all: the critique of ideology, the diagnosis of conceptual confusion, the construction of alternatives, and the articulation of what a practice would have to become in order to be defensible.

The unifying thesis of this book, then, is this:

> **Philosophy is not a catalogue of opinions but a discipline of systematic analysis — the disciplined study of what we would have to show, say, and assume in order to make our ordinary beliefs, concepts, and practices coherent.**

The three definitions are three aspects of one activity: analysis clarifies the concept, reconstruction makes explicit the practice, and the conditions-of-intelligibility question tells us what the whole thing is *for*. None of them is a definition in the sense of a set of necessary and sufficient conditions — and a reader who has already absorbed Chapter 3 will recognise that as a feature, not a bug.

**A note on the history of philosophy.** On this conception, the history of philosophy is not the subject; it is *data*. The great dead philosophers are not authorities to be cited but interlocutors to be assessed — and, as we shall see in §6, the *careers* of their questions are themselves philosophically informative. To treat Plato as an oracle is to insult him; to treat him as a colleague is to honour him.

---

## 3. The Perennial Questions and the “Permanent Problems” Illusion

Russell’s book opens with the table. He asks whether the table is really there, whether it has a colour, whether it is the same table when no one is looking. From this small domestic puzzle he derives the whole of the subject: appearance and reality, matter, mind, universals, truth, knowledge, value.

The list of Russell’s questions has proved remarkably durable. What is there? What can we know? What is a mind? What is a person? What is truth? What is good? Why is there something rather than nothing? These questions recur in every century, in every tradition, in every language in which philosophy has been done.

But the *durability* of the questions is not the same as the *permanence* of the problems, and the difference matters enormously for how we should read the history of the subject.

There is a tradition — Leibniz called it the *philosophia perennis*, Aldous Huxley popularised it as “the perennial philosophy” — according to which the great questions have been asked and answered, and the answers are essentially the same across cultures. The tradition has a grain of truth: the questions do recur. But the claim that the *problems* are permanent is a different and much stronger claim, and it is false in a way that has misled generations of students.

Consider three kinds of case.

**Case 1: The problem is transformed.** The medieval problem of universals — do general terms name real entities, or only particulars? — is recognisably the same question as the contemporary debate between realism about properties, trope theory, and nominalism (Ch. 15). But the *form* of the debate has been transformed: Ockham’s nominalism is not Quine’s, and Armstrong’s immanent realism is not Plato’s transcendent realism. The question persists; the space of answers has been reconstructed; the standards of adequacy have changed (we now demand, for example, that an account of properties explain the projectibility of predicates, not merely the possibility of predication). The problem was not solved; it was *re-engineered*.

**Case 2: The problem is dissolved.** “What is the substance of the soul?” “How many angels can dance on the head of a pin?” “Is the will free in the sense that it could have done otherwise under *exactly* the same circumstances, including the same desires?” The first presupposed a substance ontology of the mental that most of us no longer accept; the second presupposed a metaphysics of angels that no one now accepts; the third, as compatibilists have argued for three centuries (Ch. 27), may be a question whose presuppositions are incoherent. Dissolution is a form of progress — one of the most important forms — but it is not the form the naive picture recognises as progress, because it does not produce a *doctrine*.

**Case 3: The problem is answered.** This happens more often than philosophers like to admit, and the answers are often absorbed so thoroughly that they cease to look like philosophy. That there is no such thing as a “natural slave” (Aristotle’s view, and the view of much of the ancient world) is now a philosophical consensus, and the arguments that produced it — arguments about the moral irrelevance of natural endowment, about the universality of the capacity for practical reason — are philosophical arguments. That the state exists for the sake of the governed, not the governed for the sake of the state, is a philosophical achievement of the early modern period. That women have the capacity for rational agency is a philosophical achievement whose recency should chasten us. We do not notice these answers because they have become the *background* against which we ask the remaining questions.

The lesson is a distinction the reader should carry through the whole book:

> **A question can be permanent because it is deep, or because it is badly posed. The first kind deserves our labour; the second deserves our diagnosis.**

The diagnostic question is: *what would count as progress on this question?* If we can specify in advance what would count as an answer — a new distinction, a new argument, a new empirical finding, a demonstration that the question rests on a false presupposition — then the question is a real one, even if the answer is far off. If we cannot specify any such thing, we should suspect that the question is a pseudo-question, or a verbal dispute in disguise (Ch. 33, §6), or a question whose form has been inherited from a framework we no longer accept.

Two errors must be avoided here, and they are mirror images of each other.

- **Triumphalist historicism**: the view that all previous philosophy was confused, and that we have now got it right. This is almost always false, and it is usually a sign that the philosopher has not read enough history to know which of her own assumptions are historically contingent.
- **Antiquarianism**: the view that the ancients already said everything, and that our only task is to recover it. This is almost always false too, and it is usually a sign that the philosopher has not noticed how much of the ancient framework has been dismantled by subsequent work — sometimes by philosophy itself.

The truth is in the middle, and it is the truth this book tries to practise: **the questions are real, the answers are provisional, and the history of the answers is part of the evidence.**

---

## 4. Philosophy and Its Neighbours: Where the Handoff Happens

Philosophy has no proprietary subject matter. It has a proprietary *question* — the question of what is presupposed — and this question can be asked of any domain. That is why philosophy has neighbours, and why the boundaries are contested.

### Science

The standard picture is a **handoff**: philosophy generates questions; when a question becomes tractable by empirical methods, it is handed to science; philosophy moves on to the next frontier. On this picture, philosophy is the nursery of the sciences — natural philosophy became physics, moral philosophy became psychology and economics, the philosophy of mind is becoming cognitive neuroscience.

The handoff picture is largely true as history. But it is misleading as a picture of the *current* relation, for three reasons.

First, **the handoff is never complete.** Science does not merely inherit questions from philosophy; it inherits *presuppositions* that it cannot examine from within. That the future will resemble the past (Ch. 10), that the external world exists (Ch. 6), that our theories approximate the truth (Ch. 40), that the mathematics in which our theories are expressed refers to something (Ch. 43) — these are not scientific results. They are commitments that science makes, and philosophy is the discipline that examines them. This is not a criticism of science; it is a description of the division of labour. A discipline cannot audit its own foundations while standing on them.

Second, **the traffic runs both ways.** Philosophy constrains science as much as science constrains philosophy. The interpretation of quantum mechanics (Ch. 19, §5; Ch. 41) is not an empirical question; it is a question about what the formalism *means*, and it is settled by arguments about locality, determinism, and the nature of measurement. The ethics of research (Ch. 39, §6) is not an empirical question either. The philosophy of biology has changed how biologists think about species and function (Ch. 42). The influence is not one-directional.

Third, **some questions are permanently philosophical** because they are normative. No amount of empirical data settles whether a distribution is just, whether a being is a person with rights, or whether a life is meaningful (Part VII). This is not because the answers are arbitrary; it is because the answers are not *empirical*. The is/ought gap (Ch. 44, §1) is a real feature of the logical geography, and no scientific discovery closes it.

### Logic and mathematics

Philosophy of logic is not logic, and philosophy of mathematics is not mathematics. The logician proves theorems; the philosopher asks what a proof *is*, what a logical constant *means*, whether classical logic is correct, and what follows from the existence of independent set-theoretic questions (Ch. 35, Ch. 43). The relationship is intimate — the tools of logic are the philosopher’s instruments (Ch. 3, §3) — but the questions are distinct.

### Art

Philosophy of art is not art criticism, though it is informed by it. Its questions are: what is an aesthetic property? What is a work of art? Can art be a source of knowledge? (Ch. 49.) But there is a deeper connection, which the reader should notice: **philosophy itself uses literary techniques.** The thought experiment is a literary form (Ch. 3, §2); the dialogue is a genre; the essay is a genre. Philosophy’s form is not incidental to its content. A philosopher who cannot write cannot think clearly, because clarity of thought is largely clarity of formulation.

### Religion

Philosophy of religion is not theology. Theology reasons within a tradition, from premises the tradition supplies; philosophy of religion asks what can be rationally held, and by whom, and on what evidence (Ch. 50). But the relationship is not adversarial by nature. The greatest philosophers of religion — Aquinas, Maimonides, al-Ghazālī, Śaṅkara — were believers using philosophical tools to understand their faith. The philosopher’s task is not to debunk religion but to ask what religion commits one to, and whether those commitments can be sustained. The answer may be yes or no; the point is that it must be argued.

### The general lesson

Philosophy is the **residual discipline** — it takes up what other disciplines presuppose but cannot examine from within. “Residual” sounds like “leftover,” but that is the wrong metaphor. The better metaphor is **foundational**: philosophy is what you do when you ask what a practice rests on. Every practice rests on something, and the something is usually unexamined. The philosopher’s job is to examine it — not in order to replace the practice, but in order to know what the practice is committed to.

This is also why philosophy is so often *unwelcome*. A practice that is working does not want its foundations excavated. The philosopher is the person who asks, at the dinner party, whether the host actually owns the house. Sometimes the question is rude. Sometimes it is the most important question in the room.

---

## 5. The Payoff Problem

We come to the objection that has followed philosophy since Socrates: **what is it for?**

The charge takes several forms. The vulgar form: philosophy makes no progress, so it is a waste of time. The polite form: philosophy’s results are incommensurable with its ambitions — it promises wisdom and delivers distinctions. The political form: philosophy is a luxury of the leisured classes, and its questions are distractions from the practical business of living. The internal form, which is the most serious: philosophy’s own history suggests that its problems are insoluble, and a discipline with insoluble problems is either an art form or a pathology.

The answer is not that philosophy *does* make progress in the way science does. It does not, and pretending otherwise is the surest way to lose the argument. The answer is that **progress is not one thing**, and philosophy produces several kinds of it. Five are worth distinguishing.

### (i) Progress in clarity

The dissolution of a pseudo-problem is a genuine advance, even though it produces no doctrine. When Ryle (1949) argued that the “ghost in the machine” is a category mistake, he did not prove that minds are physical; he showed that a certain way of posing the mind–body problem was confused. When Wittgenstein asked what a rule is, and what following a rule consists in, he did not solve the problem of normativity; he made it possible to see what a solution would have to look like (Ch. 31, §6). When contemporary philosophers distinguish the *hard problem* of consciousness from the *easy problems* (Ch. 24), they do not solve either; they reorganise the terrain so that the hard part is visible.

This is not a consolation prize. A problem that is clearly posed is a different problem from one that is not, and the difference is practical: clear problems can be worked on, confused ones cannot.

### (ii) Progress in technique

Philosophy has produced instruments that are used far beyond philosophy: formal logic, probability theory, decision theory, the theory of definitions, the analysis of counterfactuals, the apparatus of possible worlds, the distinction between validity and soundness, the concept of a counterexample, the method of reflective equilibrium. These are not opinions; they are tools, and they work. A student who learns them can use them in law, in medicine, in public policy, in computer science, and in the ordinary business of arguing with her family.

### (iii) Progress in vision

Russell’s own answer, and still the best one. Philosophy enlarges the self by forcing it to consider alternatives to what it has always assumed. This enlargement operates in three dimensions:

- **Temporal**: the history of philosophy shows that our most obvious beliefs were once contested, and that the contest was not stupid. The reader who has understood why Aristotle defended natural slavery, and why the argument fails, has learned something about the contingency of her own moral certainties.
- **Cultural**: the non-Western traditions — Buddhist, Confucian, Indian, African, Islamic — are not decorations. They contain systematic alternatives to positions we take for granted, and some of them are better than the positions we take for granted. (This book treats them as theories, not as curiosities; see the optional threads in Parts II, III, IV, and VII.)
- **Conceptual**: philosophy teaches the imagination of alternatives. To see that our concept of *person* might be otherwise, that our concept of *cause* might be otherwise, that our concept of *justice* might be otherwise, is to be freed from the tyranny of the actual.

This is Russell’s “union with the not-self,” and it is a genuine good — not because it makes us happy, but because it makes us less parochial. A mind that has never been forced to consider a serious alternative to its own framework is not free; it is merely confident.

### (iv) Negative results are results

A great deal of philosophy consists in showing that a question cannot be answered as posed, that two apparently distinct positions collapse into one, that an argument begs the question, that a concept is incoherent, or that a debate is verbal. These are results. They change what we can say. The history of philosophy is littered with positions that are now *dead* — not because they were refuted by a single decisive argument, but because the cumulative weight of objections made them untenable. That is progress, even if it is progress by subtraction.

### (v) Self-knowledge

Philosophy articulates what we already believe, so that we can criticise it. This is the Socratic function: the unexamined life is not worth living because an unexamined life is one in which the agent does not know what she is committed to. The method of reflective equilibrium (Ch. 3, §4) is precisely the method of bringing our particular judgments and our general principles into a stable, criticisable relation. The result is not a system; it is a *self* that knows what it thinks and why.

### The honest qualification

None of this shows that *all* philosophy is valuable. A great deal of it is not. The book will try to be honest about the difference, and the criteria are not mysterious:

- Does the work **change what we can say**? (Does it introduce a distinction, close a loophole, open a question?)
- Does it **survive objections**? (Has it been tested against the strongest available counterarguments, or only against straw men?)
- Does it **connect**? (Does it bear on other domains — science, ethics, politics, ordinary life — or is it a closed game?)
- Is it **honest about its own status**? (Does it claim more certainty than it has?)

These criteria are themselves philosophical, and they are themselves contestable. That is not a defect; it is the subject matter.

---

## 6. Two Case Studies: The Careers of Questions

The best way to see what philosophy is is to watch it work. We will trace two questions across four centuries — one from ethics, one from metaphysics — and observe what happens to a question when it is asked by different people with different tools.

### Case A: “What is justice?”

**Plato (*Republic*, c. 380 BCE).** Justice is a property of a *soul* as well as of a *city*, and it consists in each part performing its proper function under the rule of reason. The question is answered by a metaphysical psychology: to know what justice is, you must know what the soul is. Justice is *harmony*; injustice is *disease*.

**Aristotle (*Nicomachean Ethics*, Book V, c. 340 BCE).** Justice is a virtue, and the central form of it is *distributive*: justice consists in proportional equality — treating equals equally and unequals unequally, in proportion to relevant difference. The question becomes: *which differences are relevant?* Aristotle’s answer (merit, and in practice, status) is one we now reject; his *form* of answer — proportional equality — remains one of the permanent options.

**Hobbes (*Leviathan*, 1651).** Justice is a matter of *convention*. There is no justice in the state of nature, because there is no property, and there is no property without a sovereign to define it. Justice becomes *artificial*: it is what the sovereign commands, and its ground is the mutual transfer of rights that constitutes political society.

**Hume (*A Treatise of Human Nature*, 1739–40).** Justice is an *artificial virtue*: it is not natural to human beings but arises from convention, and its point is *utility* — the stability of possession. The question shifts from metaphysics to *explanation*: what is the origin of the institution of justice, and what sustains it?

**Kant (*Groundwork*, 1785).** Justice is grounded in *autonomy*. A maxim is just if it can be willed as a universal law; persons are ends in themselves, never merely means. The question shifts from the *content* of justice to its *ground*: what makes a claim of justice valid? Answer: its universalizability.

**Mill (*Utilitarianism*, 1861).** Justice is a department of morality, and morality is the maximisation of happiness. Justice is the set of rules whose general observance conduces to the greatest happiness; the feeling of justice is the natural sentiment of retaliation, moralised by social sympathy. The question becomes *aggregative*.

**Rawls (*A Theory of Justice*, 1971).** Justice is the first virtue of social institutions, and the question is: which principles would free and equal persons choose behind a veil of ignorance? Answer: the two principles — equal basic liberties, and inequalities only if they benefit the least advantaged. The method shifts from intuition and metaphysics to *contract* and *reflective equilibrium*.

**Nozick (*Anarchy, State, and Utopia*, 1974).** Justice is *historical* and *entitlement-based*: a distribution is just if it arose by just acquisition and just transfer, whatever its pattern. The question shifts from *end-state* to *process*.

**Sen and Nussbaum (1980s–2000s).** Justice is about *capabilities*: what people are actually able to do and be. The question shifts from resources and welfare to *functionings*, and from the ideal to the comparative.

**Anderson (1999), Fraser, Honneth, Fricker (2007).** Justice is about *relations*: equality of standing, not merely of stuff; and the distribution of *epistemic* goods — credibility, interpretive resources — is itself a matter of justice. The question shifts from the individual to the structure of recognition.

**What changed?** The unit of analysis (soul → city → individual → basic structure → global order); the method (metaphysical psychology → convention → transcendental argument → contract → reflective equilibrium → empirical critique); the scope (who counts: citizens, property-holders, all persons, all sentient beings, future generations); and the *content* of the answer (harmony, proportion, command, utility, universal law, difference principle, entitlement, capability, standing).

**What stayed?** The question of the *ground* of normative authority — why does justice bind? The tension between equality and desert. The problem of the second-best: what justice requires when the ideal is unattainable. And the phenomenon that started it all: the *experience* of injustice, which is the data that any theory must explain.

**The lesson.** “Justice” is what W. B. Gallie (1956) called an **essentially contested concept**: a concept whose correct application is not merely uncertain but *essentially* a matter of dispute, because the dispute is part of what the concept is for. That does not make the dispute arbitrary. It makes it *permanent*, and it makes the history of the dispute part of the evidence. A theory of justice that has not learned from the failures of its predecessors is not a theory; it is a repetition.

### Case B: “What is a cause?”

**Aristotle (*Physics*, Book II).** There are four causes: material, formal, efficient, final. The question “why?” has four legitimate answers, and the philosopher’s task is to distinguish them. This is not yet a theory of *causation* in the modern sense; it is a theory of *explanation*.

**Hume (*Enquiry*, 1748).** Cause is not a relation we perceive; it is a relation we *infer*, on the basis of constant conjunction and the custom of the mind. The two definitions — priority and contiguity, and necessary connection — are the seed of the whole modern debate. Causation becomes an *empirical* relation, and the question becomes: what is the *content* of the idea of necessary connection?

**Mill (*A System of Logic*, 1843).** Causation is invariable succession, and the methods of difference, agreement, and concomitant variation are the instruments for discovering it. The question becomes *methodological*: how do we identify causes in complex circumstances?

**Russell (“On the Notion of Cause,” 1912).** The concept of cause is a relic. Physics has no use for it; the word “cause” is “so inextricably bound up with misleading associations as to make its complete extrusion from the philosophical vocabulary desirable.” The question becomes *eliminative*: should we abandon the concept altogether?

**Lewis (“Causation,” 1973).** Causation is analysed counterfactually: $c$ causes $e$ iff, had $c$ not occurred, $e$ would not have occurred (with complications for pre-emption and overdetermination). The question becomes *semantic* and *modal*.

**Woodward (*Making Things Happen*, 2003).** Causation is *intervention*: $X$ causes $Y$ if an intervention on $X$ changes $Y$. The question becomes *practical* and *manipulability*-theoretic, and it connects directly to experimental method and to the special sciences.

**Mechanists (Machamer, Darden, Craver, 2000).** Causation is the production of change by organised mechanisms; to explain is to describe the mechanism. The question becomes *structural* and *levels*-theoretic.

**Contemporary pluralism.** There is no single relation of causation; there are several — difference-making, production, dependence, mechanism — and they answer different questions (Ch. 18). The question becomes *diagnostic*: which concept of cause is in play in this context, and what work is it doing?

**What changed?** The *science* (Aristotelian physics → Newtonian mechanics → quantum mechanics and statistics); the *logic* (syllogistic → Mill’s methods → counterfactual semantics → interventionist calculus); the *ambition* (from defining the essence of cause to mapping a family of related notions).

**What stayed?** The asymmetry of causation (causes explain effects, not vice versa); the connection between causation and *responsibility* (we hold people responsible for what they cause); the problem of distinguishing causation from mere correlation; and the experience of *agency* — of making something happen — which is arguably the root of the whole concept.

**The lesson.** Sometimes the science dissolves a concept, as Russell thought it dissolved causation; sometimes the concept is reconstructed to fit the science, as the interventionists reconstructed it; sometimes the question turns out to have a plural answer, as the pluralists argue. All three outcomes are philosophical results. None of them is the outcome the naive picture predicts, because the naive picture assumes that a question either has one answer or none.

### The meta-lesson

Philosophical questions have **careers**. They are asked, answered, criticised, reformulated, abandoned, and revived. The career of a question is not a distraction from the question; it is part of what the question is. A philosopher who does not know the career of her question is likely to reinvent a wheel that was shown to be square in 1748.

This is why this book is organised around problems rather than around thinkers. The thinkers matter — Appendix D provides a chronological map — but they matter as participants in a conversation, not as monuments in a museum.

---

## Coda: How This Chapter Sets Up the Rest

We have arrived at a working conception of the subject. Philosophy is the disciplined study of the conditions of intelligibility: what we would have to show, say, and assume for our beliefs, concepts, and practices to be coherent. It proceeds by analysis, reconstruction, argument, and diagnosis. Its history is data, not authority. Its progress is real but plural: clarity, technique, vision, negative results, and self-knowledge. Its questions are permanent in some cases because they are deep and in others because they are badly posed, and the first task of the philosopher is to tell the difference.

The next three chapters supply the instruments. Chapter 2 takes apart the argument — the atom of philosophical work — and shows how to reconstruct one, attack one, and repair one. Chapter 3 surveys the toolkit: conceptual analysis, thought experiments, formalization, reflective equilibrium, genealogy, phenomenology, ordinary language, experimental philosophy, and the art of dissolution. Chapter 4 turns to the practice: how to read a paper, how to write one, how to evaluate one, and how to be honest in the process.

Only then, in Part II, do we turn to the terrain: knowledge, and its limits. The order is deliberate. The problems are intoxicating; the method is what keeps us sober. A reader who begins with the problems will have a splendid time and will believe everything she reads. A reader who begins with the method will be harder to fool — including by this book.

---

### Summary

- The **naive picture** — philosophy as a catalogue of opinions — mistakes difficulty for arbitrariness, disagreement for subjectivity, and the sociology of the discipline for its content.
- Philosophy is best understood as **systematic analysis**: the study of the conditions of intelligibility of our beliefs, concepts, and practices. Conceptual analysis and rational reconstruction are two of its instruments, not its whole nature.
- The **permanent problems** are not all permanent for the same reason. Some are deep; some are badly posed. Distinguishing them is a central philosophical skill.
- Philosophy’s relation to science is not a one-way handoff. Science inherits presuppositions it cannot audit; philosophy inherits data and constraints it cannot ignore.
- The **payoff** of philosophy is real but plural: clarity, technique, vision, negative results, and self-knowledge. Not all philosophy delivers it; the criteria for good work are themselves philosophical.
- Philosophical questions have **careers**. The history of a question is part of the evidence for its answer.

### Study Questions

1. The chapter claims that disagreement is evidence of difficulty, not of subjectivity. Is that always true? Can you construct a case in which durable disagreement *does* undermine the claim that there is a fact of the matter?
2. Which of the three definitions of philosophy (§2) do you find most defensible, and why? Can you give a case that one definition handles better than the others?
3. Identify a philosophical question that you believe has been *dissolved* rather than solved. What did the dissolution consist in, and was it progress?
4. Is the “handoff” picture of philosophy and science defensible? Give an example of a question that has been successfully handed off, and one that has not.
5. Russell thought philosophy’s value lay in its uncertainty. Is that a virtue or an admission of failure?
6. Trace a question of your own — “What is a person?”, “What is a right?”, “What is a number?” — through three historical figures, and identify what changed and what stayed.

### Further Reading

- **Primary**: Russell, *The Problems of Philosophy* (1912), Chs. I and XV — still the best short introduction to the spirit of the subject, and the text this book is in conversation with.
- **On method**: Gilbert Ryle, “Philosophical Arguments” (1945); Isaiah Berlin, “The Purpose of Philosophy” (1962); Bernard Williams, *Philosophy as a Human Discipline* (2000).
- **On the nature of the subject**: Timothy Williamson, *The Philosophy of Philosophy* (2007), for the ambitious view; Richard Rorty, *Philosophy and the Mirror of Nature* (1979), for the sceptical view; David Chalmers, “Why Isn’t There More Progress in Philosophy?” (2015), for the honest stocktaking.
- **On essentially contested concepts**: W. B. Gallie, “Essentially Contested Concepts” (1956); on conceptual engineering, Cappelen, *Fixing Language* (2018) and Haslanger, *Resisting Reality* (2012).
- **Historical orientation**: Anthony Kenny, *A New History of Western Philosophy* (2004–07), for a reliable map; Peter Adamson’s *History of Philosophy without any gaps* (podcast and books), for the non-Western traditions that most histories omit.

---

> *A closing note on method.* This chapter has argued that philosophy is a discipline, not a mood. The argument is itself philosophical, and it is therefore open to objection. That is not a defect. It is the form of intellectual honesty that the rest of the book will try to practise: state the thesis, give the argument, invite the objection, and revise. If the reader finishes this book with a set of well-formulated objections to it, the book will have succeeded.

# Chapter 2 — The Anatomy of an Argument

> “It is a very common error to suppose that the object of argument is to convince an opponent. The object of argument is to find out what is true.”
> — Attributed to many; practised by few.

---

## 1. Assertions, Questions, and the Pseudo-Question

Philosophy begins with a sentence that can be true or false. This sounds trivial. It is not. A great deal of bad philosophy, and a great deal of good philosophy gone astray, consists in treating a question as though it had a propositional answer when it does not, or treating an assertion as though it were a question when it already presupposes its own answer.

### 1.1 Three kinds of utterance

Consider three utterances:

1. *“The table is solid.”*
2. *“Is the table solid?”*
3. *“Please pass the salt.”*

Only (1) has a **truth value**. Utterance (2) is not true or false; it is a *request for information*, and it is answered by an assertion. Utterance (3) is an *action* — an order or a request — and it is assessed as appropriate or inappropriate, polite or rude, effective or ineffective, but not as true or false.

The distinction is not merely grammatical. It corresponds to a difference in **direction of fit** (Anscombe 1957; Searle 1969), which we will use repeatedly in this book (Ch. 28, §3). An assertion is supposed to fit the world: if the table is not solid, the assertion fails. A command is supposed to make the world fit it: if the salt is not passed, the command fails. Questions sit awkwardly between: they presuppose a possible answer and request the world-fitting direction.

For a working philosopher, the practical upshot is this: **before you argue, make sure you are arguing about a proposition.** Most philosophical disputes are disputes about which proposition is true. Some are disputes about which question to ask. A few are disputes about whether there is anything to dispute.

### 1.2 The pseudo-question

What is a **pseudo-question**? Not simply a question we cannot answer. “What is the mass of the universe?” is a question we may never answer; it is not thereby pseudo. A pseudo-question is a question that *appears* to have a propositional answer but in fact does not — because its presuppositions fail, or because it is a verbal dispute, or because the answer is stipulated by the question itself.

Four diagnostic types are worth distinguishing. Each is a tool, and each has its failure modes.

**(a) Presupposition failure.** “Why did the King of France invade Belgium?” presupposes that there is a King of France. If there is not, the question is not hard; it is *defective*. The right response is not to speculate about his motives but to reject the presupposition.

Russell’s theory of descriptions (Ch. 12, §2) was designed precisely to handle this. “The present King of France is bald” is analysed not as a subject–predicate sentence whose subject fails to refer, but as a conjunction of three claims:

$$\exists x(\text{King}(x) \wedge \text{France}(x) \wedge \forall y((\text{King}(y) \wedge \text{France}(y)) \to y = x) \wedge \text{Bald}(x))$$

The sentence is false (not truth-valueless), because the existential conjunct fails. The technique generalises: when a question seems unanswerable, ask **what it presupposes**, and then ask whether the presupposition is true. Often the honest answer is that the presupposition is a substantive thesis that has not been argued.

**(b) Category mistakes.** “What is the average colour of the number seven?” The question is not hard; it applies a predicate to a category of thing to which the predicate does not apply. Gilbert Ryle (1949) diagnosed the mind–body problem partly in these terms: the question “Where is the mind?” is defective if minds are not the kind of thing that has a spatial location — just as “Where is the university?” is defective if universities are not buildings (though see Ch. 23, §1, for the objection that this is too quick).

The category-mistake diagnosis is powerful but dangerous. It is too easy to declare one’s opponents guilty of a category mistake instead of answering them. The burden is on the diagnostician to say *which* category is being confused and *why* the predicate does not apply. Wittgenstein’s later method (Ch. 3, §7) is a sustained exercise in this burden.

**(c) Verbal dispute.** A dispute is verbal when the parties agree on all the facts but disagree about the meaning or use of a word. “Is a tomato a fruit?” — if both parties agree that tomatoes are the seed-bearing ovaries of a flowering plant and also that they are used in salads, the question “Is it a fruit?” is settled by stipulating which sense of “fruit” is in play.

The hard case, and the philosophically important one, is the dispute that is *partly* verbal and partly substantive. David Chalmers (2011) offers a method for diagnosing these: **ask what the parties would say if they agreed about the word.** If the disagreement evaporates, it was verbal. If a residue remains, that residue is the substantive question, and it should be stated in neutral terms. The method does not always work (it presupposes that the parties can identify what they “would say,” which is exactly what is contested), but it is a useful first pass. We will apply it to several disputes in this book, notably in Ch. 20, §7 (what would settle idealism?), Ch. 22, §5 (is metaphysics a verbal dispute?), and Ch. 33, §6.

**(d) Stipulative or trivial questions.** “Is a bachelor an unmarried man?” If “bachelor” is *defined* as “unmarried man,” the question is answered by the definition, and there is nothing to investigate. The danger is that a question that looks substantive is in fact definitional, and the investigator wastes time trying to discover the answer to a definition. Conversely, a question that looks definitional may be substantive: “Is knowledge justified true belief?” cannot be settled by definition, as Gettier showed (Ch. 7, §2), because “knowledge” is a *philosophically loaded* term whose application is precisely what is at issue.

### 1.3 The test for a genuine question

The single best test is this:

> **Can you say, in advance, what would count as an answer — and what would count as evidence for it?**

This test does not require that the answer be *available*. It requires that the *shape* of an answer be specifiable. For “What is the mass of the universe?” the shape is clear (a number in kilograms, with error bars) even though the measurement is not available. For “Why is there something rather than nothing?” the shape is much less clear — is the answer a cause, a reason, a necessity, a brute fact? — and the question’s genuineness is correspondingly contested (Ch. 14, §1). For “Is the number seven blue?” there is no shape at all, which is why we call it a pseudo-question.

The test is a *heuristic*, not a decision procedure. Some genuinely deep questions have no antecedently specifiable shape, because part of the answer is a new conception of what an answer would look like. But when a question fails the test *and* there is no independent reason to expect a conceptual innovation, we should suspect a pseudo-question.

### 1.4 A diagnostic checklist

Before beginning work on a question, run it through the following:

| Test | Question to ask | If it fails |
|---|---|---|
| **Truth-aptness** | Could the answer be true or false? | It is an order, an expression, or a performative |
| **Presupposition** | What must be the case for the question to arise? | Reject or examine the presupposition |
| **Category** | Is the predicate applicable to the subject? | Diagnose the category mistake |
| **Verbality** | Would agreement on the word settle it? | Restate substantively or declare it verbal |
| **Shape** | What would count as an answer? | Examine whether the question is well-formed |
| **Stakes** | What turns on the answer? | Distinguish intellectual from practical import |

The checklist is not a substitute for thinking; it is a way of avoiding the commonest errors in the first hour of work. We will return to it in Appendix E, where it becomes a worksheet.

---

## 2. The Premise–Conclusion Architecture

An **argument**, in the philosopher’s sense, is a set of propositions in which some (the **premises**) are offered as support for another (the **conclusion**). This is a technical sense of the word. In ordinary English, “argument” often means a quarrel. In philosophy, a quarrel may contain no arguments at all.

### 2.1 The standard form

We standardise arguments into a numbered list, with the conclusion clearly marked:

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
1. & \text{All humans are mortal.} \\
2. & \text{Socrates is a human.} \\
\hline
3. & \therefore \text{Socrates is mortal.}
\end{array}
$$

Standardisation is not pedantry. It forces the arguer to say *what exactly* is being claimed, and it exposes the *gaps*. An argument that cannot be standardised is usually an argument that has not been thought through.

**The premises may be any number, including one.** “It is raining; therefore the street is wet” has one premise and relies on an implicit generalisation. **The conclusion is one proposition** — a common error is to write a multi-sentence “conclusion” that is really two conclusions, each needing separate support. **The order is not the argument**: premises may appear after the conclusion, and the argument’s validity does not depend on presentation order.

### 2.2 Validity

An argument is **valid** if and only if it is impossible for all the premises to be true and the conclusion false. Equivalently: the conclusion follows from the premises; the premises *entail* the conclusion.

Validity is a property of the **form**, not of the content. The following two arguments have the same form and are both valid:

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
1. & \text{All cats are mammals.} \\
2. & \text{Felix is a cat.} \\
\hline
3. & \therefore \text{Felix is a mammal.}
\end{array}
\qquad\qquad
\begin{array}{ll}
1. & \text{All unicorns are immortal.} \\
2. & \text{Shadowfax is a unicorn.} \\
\hline
3. & \therefore \text{Shadowfax is immortal.}
\end{array}
$$

The second argument is valid — *if* its premises were true, its conclusion would have to be true. It is also unsound, because its premises are (probably) false. The point is worth dwelling on: **validity is cheap.** Any argument can be made valid by adding a premise. The interesting questions are whether the premises are true and whether the validity is non-trivial.

**Formal validity** is validity in virtue of logical form alone, where the form is expressed in a formal language with a semantics (Ch. 35, §2). **Material validity** (sometimes called *semantic* or *enthymematic* validity) is validity that depends on the meanings of the non-logical terms. “A is a bachelor; therefore A is unmarried” is materially valid, because of what “bachelor” means, but it is not formally valid in the language of first-order logic without adding a meaning postulate.

There is a live debate about whether all good arguments are formally valid, or whether material validity is a genuine and irreducible kind (see Brandom 1994, 2000; and the discussion of inferentialism in Ch. 31, §3). This book treats both as legitimate, but insists that formal validity is the clearer and more testable notion, and should be used wherever possible.

### 2.3 Soundness

An argument is **sound** if and only if it is valid **and** all of its premises are true. Soundness is the property you want. It is much harder to achieve than validity, because it requires you to *establish the premises*, and establishing a premise typically requires a further argument.

This generates the **regress of justification** (Ch. 8, §1). Every argument rests on premises; premises need support; support is further argument; and so on. The regress is not a refutation of the possibility of knowledge — foundationalists, coherentists, and infinitists offer competing accounts of where it stops (Ch. 8) — but it is a permanent structural feature of argument, and the philosopher must always be prepared to say *why* the premises are acceptable.

There is a stronger notion, **demonstrative soundness** (or *cogency*): a sound argument whose premises are *known* to be true, or at least *justified* for the person advancing it. This is what a good philosophical argument should aim at. A valid argument from premises that are merely asserted is not a proof; it is a sketch of a proof.

### 2.4 Deductive and ampliative inference

The distinction between **deductive** and **ampliative** inference is fundamental and frequently blurred.

| Feature | Deductive | Ampliative (inductive, abductive) |
|---|---|---|
| Conclusion follows with **necessity** | Yes | No |
| Possible for premises true and conclusion false | No | Yes |
| Information in conclusion | Contained in premises | Goes beyond premises |
| Defeasible by new evidence | No | Yes |
| Canonical example | *Modus ponens* | Enumerative induction, IBE |
| Goodness is | Validity | Strength / support |

The distinction is sometimes put as follows: deductive inference is **truth-preserving**, ampliative inference is **truth-extending**. Deduction guarantees that you will not lose truth; amplification allows you to gain it, at the cost of a risk of error.

**Induction** is the inference from observed instances to unobserved ones. *All observed emeralds are green; therefore the next emerald is green.* **Statistical syllogism**: *90% of Fs are G; a is an F; therefore (probably) a is G.* **Abduction** (inference to the best explanation): *the hypothesis H would explain the data; no available alternative explains it as well; therefore H is true.* We will treat abduction in detail in §5 below and in Ch. 10.

The classical empiricist tradition (Hume, Mill, Russell in Ch. VI) treated induction as the central ampliative inference. The twentieth century added abduction and probability theory, and the twenty-first century added a great deal of formal machinery. The structural point for now:

> **Most interesting philosophical arguments are ampliative.** They offer considerations that *support* a conclusion — that make it more probable, or more reasonable, or the best available hypothesis — without entailing it.

This has a consequence that beginning students often miss: **objecting to an ampliative argument does not require showing that the conclusion is false.** It is enough to show that the support is weaker than claimed — that the inference is not as strong as the arguer needs it to be. Conversely, defending an ampliative argument does not require showing that the premises entail the conclusion; it requires showing that the conclusion is *well-supported* relative to the alternatives.

### 2.5 The forms worth knowing

The following table lists the inference forms that appear most often in philosophical argument. Learn them; they are the grammar of the subject.

| Form | Pattern | Valid? | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Modus ponens* | $p \to q;\ p;\ \therefore q$ | Valid | The workhorse |
| *Modus tollens* | $p \to q;\ \neg q;\ \therefore \neg p$ | Valid | Often confused with denying the antecedent |
| Hypothetical syllogism | $p \to q;\ q \to r;\ \therefore p \to r$ | Valid | |
| Disjunctive syllogism | $p \vee q;\ \neg p;\ \therefore q$ | Valid | |
| Affirming the consequent | $p \to q;\ q;\ \therefore p$ | **Invalid** | Very common in bad philosophy |
| Denying the antecedent | $p \to q;\ \neg p;\ \therefore \neg q$ | **Invalid** | Equally common |
| Reductio ad absurdum | Assume $p$; derive $\bot$; $\therefore \neg p$ | Valid | The engine of most metaphysical argument |
| *Ex falso* | $\bot;\ \therefore q$ | Valid (classically) | Paraconsistent logicians demur (Ch. 35, §5) |
| Constructive dilemma | $p \vee q;\ p \to r;\ q \to s;\ \therefore r \vee s$ | Valid | |
| Universal instantiation | $\forall x Fx;\ \therefore Fa$ | Valid | |
| Existential generalisation | $Fa;\ \therefore \exists x Fx$ | Valid | |

Two forms deserve special comment because they are so often misused.

**Affirming the consequent** is the form of many bad arguments from success. “If the theory were true, it would make accurate predictions; it makes accurate predictions; therefore it is true.” This is invalid — the predictions could be accurate for other reasons. The valid version, *modus tollens*, is much weaker: “If the theory were true, it would make accurate predictions; it does not; therefore it is false.” This is why falsification (Ch. 40, §2) is logically cleaner than verification, and why the *no-miracles* argument for scientific realism (Ch. 40, §5) requires careful formulation: it is an inference to the best explanation, not a deductive argument, and must be assessed as such.

**Reductio** is the engine of most *a priori* philosophy, but it has a characteristic danger: the derived absurdity is often only absurd *given further assumptions*. When a philosopher says “this leads to absurdity,” ask: (i) what exactly is the absurdity? (ii) is it really absurd, or merely surprising? (iii) does the absurdity follow from the position alone, or from the position plus something the opponent need not accept? The best *reductios* derive a formal contradiction, or an implication that violates a principle the opponent has explicitly endorsed. The weakest derive a consequence the audience finds distasteful.

### 2.6 What validity does not give you

Three cautions, each of which will recur.

**(i) Validity is not persuasiveness.** A valid argument with premises your audience rejects persuades no one; a fallacious argument with premises your audience accepts often persuades everyone. The philosopher’s task is not to win but to be right (see §2.1 of Ch. 4 on the ethics of discourse), and the gap between the two is where most rhetoric lives.

**(ii) Validity is not relevance.** An argument can be valid and irrelevant to the question at issue. This happens constantly in philosophy: a valid argument is produced for a conclusion that is not the one under dispute. The motte-and-bailey (Ch. 4, §2) is the pathological form.

**(iii) Validity is not soundness, and soundness is not knowledge.** You can have a sound argument whose premises you believe for bad reasons, and a valid argument whose conclusion you cannot know because the premises are merely probable. The epistemologist’s question — *is this a good way to form the belief?* — is not answered by logic alone (Ch. 8).

---

## 3. Hidden Premises and the Principle of Charity

### 3.1 Enthymemes

Most real arguments are **enthymematic**: they leave premises unstated because they are obvious, or because the arguer has not noticed them, or because stating them would invite objection. The classic example:

> “Socrates is a man; therefore he is mortal.”

The suppressed premise is *(all men are mortal)*. Without it, the argument is invalid. With it, the argument is valid — and the question becomes whether the premise is true, which is a different question from whether the conclusion follows.

The task of reconstruction is therefore twofold: **make the argument valid** (supply the missing premises), and **make it assessable** (state the premises in a form whose truth can be evaluated). These two aims can conflict. A premise sufficient to make the argument valid may be so weak that it is uninteresting, or so strong that it is obviously false. A premise sufficient to make the argument interesting may be too weak to make it valid.

**Example.** Consider:

> “If determinism is true, no one could have done otherwise. Therefore determinism is incompatible with free will.”

Reconstruction 1 (minimal): *(If determinism is true, no one could have done otherwise; if no one could have done otherwise, determinism is incompatible with free will; therefore …)* — valid, but the second premise simply restates the conclusion. Useless.

Reconstruction 2 (substantive): *(Free will requires the ability to do otherwise; determinism excludes the ability to do otherwise; therefore free will and determinism are incompatible.)* — valid, and the premises are substantive and contestable. This is the reconstruction to work with, because it exposes the *real* dispute: whether free will requires the ability to do otherwise (Ch. 27, §2).

The skill is choosing the reconstruction that makes the argument **strongest but not stronger than the evidence allows** — and then saying which reconstruction you are using.

### 3.2 The underdetermination of reconstruction

Here is a hard truth: **the missing premises are usually underdetermined by the text.** Many different premise sets will make the argument valid. Which one “the” argument is cannot be read off the words; it requires an interpretive judgment about what the arguer *meant* or *would have accepted*.

This is a special case of the general problem of interpretation (Ch. 31, §6). It has three practical consequences.

1. **State your reconstruction explicitly**, and mark it as a reconstruction. “On the most charitable reading, the argument is …” is honest; “The argument is …” is often a fiction.
2. **Consider multiple reconstructions** before settling. The best objection to an argument may target a reconstruction other than the one you first saw.
3. **Check the reconstruction against the arguer’s other commitments.** If the reconstruction requires a premise the arguer explicitly denies elsewhere, it is probably wrong.

### 3.3 The principle of charity

The **principle of charity** (Wilson 1959; Quine 1960; Davidson 1974) says: interpret a speaker so as to maximise the truth or reasonableness of what she says, consistent with the evidence of what she actually said. The rationale is partly semantic — radical interpretation is only possible if we assume mostly-true beliefs and mostly-valid inferences — and partly methodological: the point of engaging with an argument is to engage with its *best* version.

Charity operates at three levels:

| Level | What is charitably interpreted | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Semantic** | The meanings of the words | Reading “free” as “uncoerced” rather than “uncaused” when context suggests it |
| **Logical** | The inferential connections | Supplying the missing premise rather than declaring the argument invalid |
| **Substantive** | The plausibility of the premises | Choosing the reading under which the premises are defensible |

Charity is not the same as **agreement**, and it is not the same as **weakness**. To interpret an argument charitably is to engage with its strongest form, which is the opposite of making it easy to refute. A charitable reconstruction often makes an argument *harder* to answer.

### 3.4 The limits of charity

Charity has limits, and they are important, because a principle without limits becomes a licence.

**Limit 1: fidelity to the text.** Charity cannot license a reconstruction that the arguer’s words will not bear. If the text says “all men are mortal” and you reconstruct it as “most men are mortal,” you have not interpreted; you have replaced. The principle is *charitable interpretation*, not *charitable invention*.

**Limit 2: the arguer’s own standards.** An argument must be assessed by the standards the arguer accepts, or by standards that can be argued for. If a philosopher claims deductive certainty, it is not charitable to reconstruct her argument as a probabilistic one; it is a change of subject.

**Limit 3: the possibility of error.** Sometimes the charitable reading is not the correct one, because the arguer really did make a mistake. Over-charity obscures real errors, and real errors are worth finding. The historian of philosophy has a special obligation here: the point of reading Leibniz is partly to see *what he actually thought*, including what he got wrong.

**Limit 4: the strategic use of charity.** Charity is a virtue of the interpreter, not a demand the arguer can make. “You’re not reading me charitably” is sometimes a legitimate complaint and sometimes a way of avoiding a real objection. The test is whether the uncharitable reading is *available* to a competent reader of the text.

The balanced position, which this book adopts, is what we might call **strong charity**: reconstruct the argument in its strongest form that the text will bear, state the reconstruction explicitly, and then criticise it — and, having criticised it, ask whether the arguer had a reply available.

---

## 4. Argument Maps, Dialectical Trees, and Steel-Manning

### 4.1 Argument maps

Prose is a poor medium for arguments. It hides structure, encourages irrelevance, and makes it hard to see where the weight of an argument lies. **Argument mapping** is the remedy.

An argument map represents:

- **Nodes**: propositions (premises, sub-conclusions, conclusions).
- **Support links**: one node supports another (drawn as an arrow from premise to conclusion).
- **Attack links**: an objection attacks a premise or an inference.
- **Co-premises**: premises that support *jointly* rather than independently.

The last distinction is the most important and the most often missed. Consider:

> “The butler was in the house at 10 p.m. And he had a motive. So he probably did it.”

The two premises support the conclusion *independently*: either alone raises the probability. Now consider:

> “All ravens are black. This bird is a raven. So this bird is black.”

The premises support the conclusion *jointly*: neither alone gives any support, and the support exists only in combination. In a map, joint premises are bracketed together; independent premises are separate arrows.

**Why it matters.** If premises are independent, refuting one leaves the argument standing (weakened). If they are joint, refuting one destroys the argument entirely. A great deal of philosophical confusion consists in attacking a joint premise as though it were independent, or defending an independent premise as though it were joint.

```
                 [Butler had opportunity]
                            \
                             v
                    [Butler probably did it]
                             ^
                            /
                    [Butler had motive]
```
*(Independent support)*

```
                 [All ravens are black] ─┐
                                        ├─> [This bird is black]
                 [This bird is a raven] ─┘
```
*(Joint support)*

The technique generalises to disagreements: a **dialectical map** adds the opponent’s counterarguments, the replies to those, and so on. The result is a tree whose depth is the depth of the debate.

### 4.2 The Toulmin model and its limits

Stephen Toulmin (*The Uses of Argument*, 1958) proposed a six-part analysis of argument: **claim**, **grounds**, **warrant**, **backing**, **qualifier**, **rebuttal**. The model is well known in rhetoric and informal logic, and it is useful for noticing things that the premise–conclusion model obscures — especially the *warrant* (the general principle licensing the inference) and the *qualifier* (how strongly the conclusion is claimed).

But the Toulmin model has two problems for philosophical purposes. First, it is not a formal model: there is no semantics, no definition of validity, no decision procedure. Second, it obscures the fact that warrants are themselves premises, and can be attacked as premises. For most philosophical work, the premise–conclusion model with explicit hidden premises is clearer. Toulmin’s contribution is best treated as a **checklist** — have you stated the warrant? have you qualified the conclusion? have you considered rebuttals? — rather than as an alternative logic.

### 4.3 Steel-manning

The **straw man** is the fallacy of refuting a weaker version of an opponent’s position than the one she holds. Its epidemiology is a chapter in the psychology of persuasion (Ch. 4, §2), not of logic; but its philosophical form is important because it can be committed in good faith.

**Steel-manning** is the deliberate practice of constructing the strongest version of the opponent’s position before criticising it. It has a structure:

1. **Reconstruct** the position in its most defensible form, using the charitable method of §3.
2. **Strengthen** it: add premises or distinctions that the opponent did not state but would accept; remove irrelevant or unfortunate formulations; repair obvious slips.
3. **State it back** to the opponent, or to the reader, as the target of criticism.
4. **Criticise the strengthened version**, and only then return to the actual text.

The fourth step is essential. A steel man is not a substitute for reading the text; it is a *testing procedure*. The philosophical value of steel-manning is that it converts a disagreement into a genuine test: if the strongest version survives your objection, your objection was not good enough.

**The limits of steel-manning.** Steel-manning can become a form of avoidance, if the strengthened position is so far from the actual one that criticising it is irrelevant. The rule of thumb: *the steel man should be a position the opponent would recognise as hers.* If she would say “that’s not what I meant,” you have gone too far.

### 4.4 The motte-and-bailey (preview)

A pattern to watch for, discussed fully in Ch. 4, §2: the arguer defends a **bailey** (a strong, interesting, controversial claim) in good times, and retreats to a **motte** (a weak, obvious, easily defended claim) when attacked — then returns to the bailey once the attack is over. Example: “Consciousness is a fundamental feature of the universe” (bailey) / “We don’t know how consciousness arises” (motte). The pattern is not always dishonest — sometimes the bailey is genuinely uncertain and the motte is all that can be supported — but the transition must be argued, not assumed.

---

## 5. Explanation versus Argument

Much philosophical writing confuses two different activities. The confusion is worth a section of its own, because the diagnostic payoff is large.

### 5.1 The distinction

An **argument** aims to establish the truth of a proposition. An **explanation** aims to make a phenomenon intelligible — to say *why* it is the case, or *how* it came to be, or *what* it consists in.

| | Argument | Explanation |
|---|---|---|
| Target | A proposition (the conclusion) | A phenomenon (the explanandum) |
| Success condition | Truth-preservation / support | Intelligibility / understanding |
| Canonical question | “Is it true?” | “Why is it so?” |
| Structure | Premises → conclusion | Explanans → explanandum |
| Failure mode | Invalidity, false premise | Circularity, redescription, vacuity |
| Assessed by | Logic + epistemology | Explanatory virtues (§5.3) |

The distinction is not absolute. An explanation can be offered *as* an argument (the fact that theory $T$ explains the data is a premise for the truth of $T$), and an argument can have explanatory force. But the criteria of assessment are different, and confusing them produces two characteristic errors.

**Error 1: offering an explanation where an argument is required.** “Why do you believe in God? — Because belief in God explains the religious experience.” This may or may not be a good explanation; but as an argument for the *existence* of God, it needs the further premise that the explanation is *better* than the alternatives (Ch. 50, §2), and that premise is doing all the work.

**Error 2: demanding an argument where an explanation is what is on offer.** Moral philosophy often offers *explanations* of why we have the moral beliefs we do (Gibbard, Haidt, Joyce). These are not arguments against morality; they are natural histories. Whether they are *debunking* explanations depends on further normative premises (Ch. 44, §6; Ch. 3, §5).

### 5.2 Explanans and explanandum

In the standard terminology:

- The **explanandum** is the thing to be explained — a fact, event, regularity, or phenomenon.
- The **explanans** is the set of propositions or factors that do the explaining.

Two structural points about the relation:

**(i) The asymmetry of explanation.** Explanations are asymmetric: the height of the mercury explains the reading on the thermometer, not vice versa; the past explains the present, not vice versa (though final causes make trouble for this, Ch. 42, §2). Arguments are not asymmetric in the same way: if $p$ entails $q$, and $q$ entails $p$, both entailments are valid, whereas only one direction of explanation is correct. This is one reason explanation is a genuinely different notion from inference.

**(ii) The contrast-class problem.** Why-questions are always implicitly contrastive: *why this rather than that?* “Why did the bridge collapse?” can mean: why did *this* bridge collapse (rather than standing), why did it collapse *now* (rather than later), why did it collapse *from metal fatigue* (rather than from an earthquake)? Each contrast generates a different explanandum and a different explanation (van Fraassen 1980; Ch. 38, §5). Most bad explanations in philosophy answer a different contrast question from the one that was asked.

### 5.3 Inference to the best explanation

**Abduction**, or **inference to the best explanation** (IBE), is the inference from the fact that a hypothesis would explain some body of evidence to the conclusion that the hypothesis is true (or probably true, or worthy of belief). Formally:

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
1. & H_1 \text{ explains the evidence } E \text{ better than any available alternative.} \\
2. & \text{If a hypothesis explains the evidence better than any available alternative, it is probably true.} \\
\hline
3. & \therefore H_1 \text{ is probably true.}
\end{array}
$$

The scheme is notoriously contestable. The second premise is the **principle of IBE**, and it is not a logical truth; it is a substantive methodological claim. Much of the philosophy of science in the last fifty years has been an attempt to say what “better explanation” means (Lipton 2004; Harman 1965; Psillos 2002).

The standard **explanatory virtues** are the following:

| Virtue | What it means | Warning |
|---|---|---|
| **Explanatory scope** | Explains more of the data | Can be gamed by vacuous generality |
| **Simplicity** | Fewer entities, posits, or parameters | “Simple” is theory-relative |
| **Conservatism** | Fits with what we already believe | Conservatism can entrench error |
| **Fertility** | Suggests new predictions or lines of inquiry | Speculative fertility is cheap |
| **Precision** | Makes definite, testable claims | Vague claims are unfalsifiable |
| **Mechanism** | Says *how* the explanation works | “Mechanism” is contested in the special sciences (Ch. 38, §2) |
| **Unification** | Subsumes many phenomena under one principle | Unification without truth is a fiction |

The virtues can conflict. A simple hypothesis may be less explanatory; a fertile one may be less conservative. The choice of weights is a substantive methodological decision, and there is no algorithm for it — which is precisely why IBE is both indispensable and vulnerable.

**The circularity worry.** IBE is used to justify scientific realism (the no-miracles argument); but the no-miracles argument is an application of IBE; and if IBE is not truth-conducive, the argument fails. The worry is that the justification of IBE cannot itself be an IBE without circularity (Ch. 40, §5). The best current reply is that IBE is justified pragmatically or by its track record, not by a further IBE (Psillos; Douven); the debate is live.

**The van Fraassen challenge.** Bas van Fraassen (1980) argues that the explanatory virtues are *pragmatic*, not *epistemic*: they make a theory useful or attractive, not more likely to be true. If he is right, IBE is not an inference to truth at all, but a heuristic for theory choice. This is one of the deepest disagreements in the philosophy of science, and we shall return to it in Ch. 38 and Ch. 40.

**The methodological point for the rest of this book.** Many of the most important arguments in philosophy are IBE arguments in disguise: the argument from consciousness, the argument from evil, the argument from religious experience, the no-miracles argument, the argument from the success of mathematics. Each can be reconstructed as an IBE, and each is vulnerable to the same questions: *Is the explanatory comparison fair? Are all the alternatives on the table? Are the virtues being applied consistently?* The skill of reconstructing an IBE — and of attacking one — is one of the most valuable in the subject.

### 5.4 Possibility arguments

A special and under-discussed form of argument deserves mention here, because it is everywhere in philosophy.

A **possibility argument** aims to establish a conclusion about what is *possible* or *conceivable*, not about what is actual. Its form is:

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
1. & \text{It is possible that } p \text{ (or: } p \text{ is conceivable, or not ruled out).} \\
2. & \text{If } p \text{ is possible, then } q \text{ is false (or: } q \text{ is not necessary).} \\
\hline
3. & \therefore q \text{ is false (or: } q \text{ is not necessary).}
\end{array}
$$
